To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the decision to not release transgenic sugar beet was correct, (2) the annual net benefits forgone by the de facto moratoria are in the order 169 million euro per year, (3) the annual net private irreversible costs are in the order one euro per household, and (4) the annual net public costs of the de facto moratorias are in the order zero.
the de facto moratourium of the European Union on transgenic sugar beet was the right decision, if households value the possible annual costs with about one euro or more on average.
the 1998 decision of the EU to de facto stop the release of herbicide tolerant transgenic sugar beet is correct, if the value of the possible annual irreversible costs is at least 1 Euro per hectare.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much a society should be willing to pay in terms of foregone benefits to avoid the possibility of a future transgenic sugar beet crop.
the question how much the EU is willing to pay for biodiversity conservation.
the question how the decision on the release of transgenic sugar beet should be made, and how the decision can be made in a cost-efficient way.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the de facto moratoria on herbicide tolerant sugar beets were correct, if households are willing to pay about 1 Euro per year for the option to avoid herbicide tolerant sugar.
the de facto moratium is correct if the value of annual irreversible costs exceeds 1 Euro on average.
the decision to not release transgenic sugar beet was correct if households value possible irreversible annual costs of transgenic sugar beet with about one Euro per tonne of sugar beet produced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the de facto moratorim was a good decision for society.
the EU decision was correct, as long as households value the annual irreversible costs of sugar beet with about one Euro or more.
if the EU decides to release herbicide tolerant sugar beets in the future, it would have to compensate the farmers for the irreversible costs of the decision.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the de facto moratourium of the EU on herbicide tolerant sugar beets was correct from a real option perspective.
the decision of whether to lift or not the moratorium should be made on the basis of the value that households attach to the irreversible costs of the transgenic crop.
the decision to release transgenic sugar beet should be based on the value of the option to delay release and on the value of irreversible costs.
